title: Ὄνος καὶ ἀλεκτρυὼν καὶ λέων
titleEn: The Donkey, the Cock and the Lion
part: The Donkey, the Cock and the Lion (Chambry 269)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 269. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A cock was once feeding together with a donkey.
sentences.n: συμβόσκομαι takes the dative of the companion. The cock is not at grass in any strict sense; the verb only puts the two at feed side by side, which is all the fable needs.

sentences.t: Λέοντος δ’ ἐπελθόντος τῷ ὄνῳ, ὁ ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφώνησε· καὶ ὁ μὲν λέων (φασὶ γὰρ τοῦτον τὴν τοῦ ἀλεκτρυόνος φωνὴν φοβεῖσθαι) ἔφυγεν.
sentences.tr: Leontos d’ epelthontos tōi onōi, ho alektryōn ephōnēse· kai ho men leōn (phasi gar touton tēn tou alektryonos phōnēn phobeisthai) ephygen.
sentences.l: And a lion having come upon the donkey, the cock crowed; and the lion (for they say that he fears the cock's voice) fled.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is the storyteller stepping forward: φασί, 'they say', marks it as received lore rather than something seen in the tale. ἐπέρχομαι with the dative is to come at someone with hostile intent. The μέν here finds its answering δέ only in the next sentence's ὁ δ’ ὄνος.

sentences.t: Ὁ δ’ ὄνος, νομίσας δι’ αὐτὸν πεφευγέναι, ἐπέδραμεν εὐθὺς τῷ λέοντι.
sentences.tr: Ho d’ onos, nomisas di’ auton pepheugenai, epedramen euthys tōi leonti.
sentences.l: But the donkey, having supposed that he had fled because of him, ran at once at the lion.
sentences.n: The perfect infinitive πεφευγέναι reports the flight as a fact standing there to be accounted for — and the donkey accounts for it wrongly. δι’ αὐτόν, 'because of him', is exactly the ambiguity the fable needs: because of the donkey, he thinks; because of the cock, in truth.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ πόρρω τοῦτον ἐδίωξεν, ἔνθα μηκέτι ἡ τοῦ ἀλεκτρυόνος ἐφικνεῖτο φωνή, στραφεὶς ὁ λέων τοῦτον κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Hōs de porrō touton ediōxen, entha mēketi hē tou alektryonos ephikneito phōnē, strapheis ho leōn touton katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And when he had chased him far off, to where the cock's voice no longer reached, the lion, having turned about, made a feast of him.
sentences.n: στραφείς is the aorist passive of στρέφω doing intransitive duty — 'having turned himself round', not 'having been turned'. κατεθοινήσατο is strong: to make a banquet of a thing, with κατα- meaning down to the last of it.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ θνῄσκων ἐβόα· « Ἄθλιος ἐγὼ καὶ ἀνόητος· πολεμιστῶν γὰρ μὴ ὢν γονέων, τίνος χάριν εἰς πόλεμον ἐξωρμήθην ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de thnēiskōn eboa· « Athlios egō kai anoētos· polemistōn gar mē ōn goneōn, tinos charin eis polemon exōrmēthēn ; »
sentences.l: And he, dying, kept crying out: « Wretched am I, and senseless; for being not of warlike parents, for the sake of what did I rush out to war? »
sentences.i: And as he died he cried out: « Wretched I am, and witless; born of no fighting stock, what did I go rushing off to war for? »
sentences.n: πολεμιστῶν γονέων is a genitive of origin: not born of fighting parents. μή, not οὐ, with the participle, because the reason is conceived as a condition — 'given that I am not'. τίνος χάριν is the ordinary 'for what reason'. ἐξωρμήθην is passive in form and active in sense, as often with verbs of setting out. The space before the Greek question mark is Chambry's French printing habit, kept here as part of his page.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ταπεινουμένοις ἐπίτηδες τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἐπιτίθενται, καὶ οὕτως ὑπ’ ἐκείνων ἀπόλλυνται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti polloi tōn anthrōpōn tapeinoumenois epitēdes tois echthrois epitithentai, kai houtōs hyp’ ekeinōn apollyntai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that many among men set upon enemies who are humbling themselves on purpose, and so are destroyed by them.
sentences.n: ἐπιτίθεμαι in the middle takes the dative of the party attacked. ἐπίτηδες, 'on purpose', is the sting of the moral: the low posture is a feint — and the lion of this fable was never afraid of the donkey at all.
